title: During Carnival
author: Salon
note: Carnival noise above; the last brick set with intimate care below. After Poe, The Cask of Amontillado, 1846.

scenes.title: The cellar
scenes.reentry: I did not announce what Fortunato had done to me.

breaths.text: I did not announce what Fortunato had done to me.
Announcements are for people who want witnesses.
I wanted a wall.
He had smiled through a year of small humiliations—my name mispronounced in rooms that mattered, a deal whispered away, a joke at my expense that traveled farther than apology ever would.
I bore it the way one bears damp in an old house: silently, taking measurements.
Carnival gave me cover.
Carnival gave him thirst and pride.
The Quarter flooded with glitter, cheap beads, and the smell of sugar burned into night air.
A brass band turned a corner and took the street with it.
Fortunato wore a jester's cap with bells that laughed whenever he moved, and a coat open to the humid cold.
He was drunk enough to be generous and vain enough to be led by anyone who questioned his taste.
I found him beneath a balcony dripping with plastic pearls and greeted him as a friend—because I had practiced friendship for months, carefully, until he took my arm without thinking.
"I bought a cask," I told him, pitching my voice toward embarrassment, almost shame.
"Amontillado.
Mid-carnival, of all times.
I'm not sure it's genuine.
Luchresi said he'd come look tonight, but—"
Fortunato's face pinched at the name.
Pride is a leash if you know where to stand.
"Luchresi cannot tell Amontillado from cooking sherry," he said.
"Show me.
Now. Before the night gets stupid."
The bells agreed, bright and idiotic.
We left the music behind by degrees—first the drums, then the horns, then only our footsteps, his cough, and a scooter beeping somewhere as if startled.
My family's old building kept a cellar that held wine, brick, and a damp that never left the bones of the place.
On the stairs I offered him a bottle for his throat.
He drank and toasted the buried and the soon-to-be-drunk.
I smiled in the dark where he could not quite see my mouth.
Deeper. The air grew colder and mineral, like a mouthful of coins.
I showed him niches, bottles gray with dust, a trowel left among stones as if a workman had stepped away for a smoke.
Water ticked somewhere in the walls.
At the end of a narrow crypt I gestured to a recess barely wider than a man.
"There," I said.
"If it's anything, it's there."
He stepped in, unsteady, merry, already composing the lecture he would give me about vintage and trust.
In a moment I had him against the granite.
The chain went around his waist with a sound like heavy jewelry.
The padlock clicked—small, polite, final.
His bells rang once in surprise.
Dust sifted from the ceiling onto his shoulders like cheap snow.
"This is a joke," he said, still half laughing, as if Carnival could not end in a cellar, as if I were still the man who absorbed insults for sport.
"Yes," I said, and began the wall.
Brick after brick.
Mortar wet on my gloves, gray as river fog.
At first he pleaded with jokes, then with my first name spoken softly, then with threats that had no legs in the dark.
Then he wept in a way that would have moved someone else—someone who had not already chosen the last brick.
I worked without hurry.
From the street far above, Carnival thundered on—horns, a sudden cheer, someone screaming with joy that belonged to another plot entirely.
When only a single opening remained, I held the lantern close so he could see my face, calm, almost tender, the face of a host at the end of a long party.
"For the love of God, Montresor!" he cried.
"Yes," I said.
"For the love of God."
I set the last brick with care and stepped back into the dark that now belonged only to me.
I called his name once, for form.
The bells did not answer.
Only the drip in the walls, and my own breathing, steady as the mortar cooling.
Years later I still walk past the building during Carnival.
Beads click underfoot.
A shared scooter lies abandoned near the curb, one wheel still spinning.
Under the music I hear nothing from the cellar—only, if I stand long enough, the remembered drip, and the place where his bells went quiet.
